subject: Tokenizer fertility asymmetry as a confound in cross-lingual transfer benchmarks for low-resource language adaptation
prompt:
Topic: Tokenizer fertility asymmetry as a confound in cross-lingual transfer benchmarks for low-resource language adaptation

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1921)
response:
Tokenizer fertility — the number of tokens a tokenizer produces per word — varies dramatically across languages, and this variation is not random: it systematically disadvantages languages that were underrepresented in the tokenizer's training corpus. When you benchmark a multilingual model on, say, cross-lingual transfer from English to Yoruba or Quechua, a low-resource target language may fragment into three to five times as many subword tokens as the English source, consuming disproportionate sequence-length budget and diluting the positional and attention signal that the model uses to encode meaning. The central question is whether observed performance gaps between high- and low-resource languages in transfer benchmarks reflect genuine model incapacity or are partially an artifact of this tokenization asymmetry — a measurement confound that makes the model look worse on low-resource languages than it actually is, or differently bad for the wrong reasons. What a beginner misses is that fertility asymmetry doesn't just slow things down; it changes the granularity of representation (morpheme boundaries become arbitrary), creates spurious vocabulary overlaps that mislead the model about cognate relationships, and means that sequence truncation at a fixed context window bites much harder for some languages than others. An expert worries specifically about benchmark validity: if you report a 15-point accuracy gap between English and a low-resource language on a span-extraction task, you cannot cleanly attribute that gap to transfer difficulty without controlling for the fact that the answer span in the low-resource language may occupy twice as many tokens, shifting probability mass in ways that have nothing to do with linguistic or semantic transfer.

If you wanted to empirically isolate the fertility confound from genuine transfer difficulty in an existing benchmark, what would a controlled experiment look like — and what would you have to hold constant?

The cleanest design would hold model weights, training data, and task constant while varying only the tokenizer, using a fixed-fertility resampling scheme: for each evaluation example, you truncate or pad token sequences so every language presents exactly the same number of tokens to the model, then compare downstream accuracy. Concretely, you could take XQuAD or MLQA — span extraction benchmarks with parallel data across 10-11 languages — and evaluate the same mBERT or XLM-R checkpoint under three conditions: its native SentencePiece tokenizer (where Swahili or Turkish fertility runs roughly 2-3× English), a language-specific tokenizer trained on that language alone retokenized into the model's embedding space via vocabulary projection, and a fertility-normalized oracle that artificially equalizes sequence length by subword merging. Chung et al. (2020) on "Improving and Simplifying" multilingual tokenization and the Rust et al. (2021) "How Good Is Your Tokenizer?" paper both gesture at this but don't run the fully controlled ablation — Rust et al. show fertility correlates with downstream performance (r ≈ 0.85 on some tasks) but correlation isn't isolation. What you must hold constant is tricky: vocabulary overlap between source and target languages (since retraining a tokenizer changes which wordpieces are shared, altering transfer pathways independently of fertility), the number of training examples seen per language during pretraining, and crucially the position of the answer span within the token sequence, because span-extraction accuracy degrades near truncation boundaries in ways that interact with fertility nonlinearly. The hardest thing to control is that any tokenizer change partially redefines what the model's existing embeddings mean — you can't truly swap tokenizers post-hoc without either retraining embeddings or accepting that you've introduced a second confound alongside the one you're trying to isolate.

subject: Tokenizer fertility asymmetry as a confound in cross-lingual transfer benchmarks for low-resource language adaptation
prompt:
Given that vocabulary overlap between source and target languages is itself partly a product of tokenizer design, how do you distinguish whether cross-lingual transfer is happening through shared subword pieces versus through deeper contextual representations — and does fertility asymmetry affect those two pathways differently?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-1923)

The standard dissection uses "zero-overlap" transfer pairs — language combinations that share essentially no subword vocabulary — as a natural ablation: if mBERT transfers reasonably to languages like Japanese or Swahili from English despite near-zero lexical overlap, the transfer must be flowing through structural/contextual representations rather than shared pieces, and Pires et al. (2019) showed exactly this, with mBERT achieving non-trivial NER transfer to languages with completely disjoint scripts. A more surgical method is the "embedding surgery" approach from Tran (2020) and later Minixhofer et al. (2022) with "WECHSEL": you replace a model's entire embedding matrix with target-language-specific vectors trained separately, then freeze them and fine-tune only the transformer layers — if performance holds, the contextual layers were doing the work; if it collapses, the pretrained embeddings were load-bearing. Fertility asymmetry almost certainly affects these two pathways differently: the shared-subword pathway is directly disrupted when a morphologically rich low-resource language shatters into many pieces, because the shared pieces that survive tend to be punctuation, digits, and borrowed vocabulary rather than content-bearing morphemes, making the overlap semantically shallow even when numerically present. The contextual pathway is hurt in a subtler, positional way — high fertility means the model's attention heads must route information across more token positions to reconstruct a single word's meaning, and the cross-lingual alignment of contextual representations (which Libovický et al. 2020 showed is surprisingly strong in middle layers of mBERT) degrades when the "same" sentence occupies very different position structures in two languages. What this means practically is that fertility asymmetry likely causes a qualitative shift in which transfer pathway dominates: for low-fertility language pairs the model can lean on subword overlap as a scaffold, but for high-fertility low-resource targets it's forced to rely entirely on contextual alignment that was itself learned from skewed data — and benchmarks don't currently report which pathway is active, making failure mode diagnosis nearly impossible.

Fine-tuning on a source language task does measurably damage cross-lingual alignment, and this is not speculative — Merchant et al. (2020) showed that fine-tuning mBERT on English MNLI causes representational drift in middle layers that degrades zero-shot transfer to other languages, with the effect concentrated in the layers that Libovický et al. identified as most cross-lingually aligned, essentially overwriting the general-purpose alignment with task-specific English geometry. The mechanism is that fine-tuning sharpens attention patterns toward English-specific syntactic and lexical cues that don't generalize — heads that were tracking loose cross-lingual structural correspondences get repurposed to track, say, English negation markers or hypothesis-premise lexical overlap, which are surface features with no reliable cross-lingual analog. Fertility asymmetry likely modulates this damage through sequence length effects on attention entropy: in a high-fertility target language, the same semantic content is spread across more tokens, so attention heads calibrated on compact English representations must generalize across a much sparser token graph — the fine-tuned heads are not just wrong but wrong in a way that scales with how fragmented the target language is. Concrete evidence for modulation comes indirectly from Lauscher et al. (2020) on "zero-shot cross-lingual transfer," which found that transfer performance degradation after fine-tuning correlates with typological distance, and fertility is partially a proxy for that distance — but the paper doesn't decompose fertility specifically, which is precisely the gap. The practical implication is alarming: standard fine-tune-on-English-then-evaluate-on-target pipelines may be actively hostile to high-fertility low-resource languages in a way that compounds the original tokenization disadvantage, meaning reported benchmark numbers for those languages reflect a model that has been both undertrained on them and then fine-tuned away from the representations that could have helped.

response:
Adapter-based methods do preserve cross-lingual alignment better than full fine-tuning — Pfeiffer et al. (2020) with "MAD-X" showed this directly, demonstrating that stacking a task adapter (trained on English) on top of a language adapter (trained on target-language MLM) with frozen base layers outperforms full fine-tuning on zero-shot transfer for low-resource languages on XNLI and NER, with the gap widening for more typologically distant languages. The preservation mechanism is straightforward: frozen middle layers retain the cross-lingual geometry that full fine-tuning erodes, and the adapter bottleneck forces the task signal to be expressed in a space that remains anchored to the pretrained representations. However, freezing introduces a different asymmetry that interacts with fertility in a specific way: the language adapters in MAD-X are trained on raw text MLM, which means a high-fertility language's adapter is learning to reconstruct heavily fragmented token sequences — the adapter is doing more representational work per word than a low-fertility language's adapter, and its capacity (typically 64-256 hidden dimensions per bottleneck) may be insufficient to compress that additional complexity, creating a capacity asymmetry that the method doesn't account for. Üstün et al. (2022) with "UDapter" and related work on cross-lingual adapter transfer hints at this problem by showing that adapter performance degrades for languages with sparse pretraining data even when base layers are frozen, but again fertility is not isolated as the explanatory variable — the confound persists. The sharpest remaining problem is that adapter size is typically set uniformly across languages as a hyperparameter, meaning the method implicitly assumes equal representational load per token across languages — an assumption that fertility asymmetry directly violates, and which could be tested by training fertility-scaled adapters (larger bottleneck for higher-fertility languages) and measuring whether the transfer gap closes proportionally.

Shared task adapters trained across multiple languages almost certainly impose a representational compromise that falls disproportionately on high-fertility languages, because the adapter's fixed capacity must simultaneously encode task-relevant features for languages whose token granularity differs by a factor of 3-5x — the adapter is effectively forced to learn a token-level task representation calibrated to the dominant (usually low-fertility, high-resource) languages in the training mix. Pfeiffer et al.'s MAD-X framework uses language-specific adapters but a single shared task adapter, which means the task adapter sees language-normalized representations from the language adapter beneath it — this partially buffers the fertility problem, but only to the extent that the language adapter successfully normalizes fertility differences, which as noted above is exactly where capacity constraints bite hardest. Concrete evidence for harmful sharing comes from Ansell et al. (2021) on "MAD-G," which generates adapters for unseen languages via typological feature vectors and shows systematic underperformance for languages with high morphological complexity — a strong proxy for fertility — suggesting the shared adapter space cannot accommodate the representational demands of those languages even when language-specific components are present. The damage mechanism is specific: in a shared task adapter, gradient updates from low-fertility languages during training will dominate simply because they produce more stable, lower-variance token-level signals, pushing the adapter weights toward representations that are suboptimal for high-fertility languages in a way analogous to but distinct from standard class imbalance — it's granularity imbalance. What makes this actively harmful rather than merely suboptimal is that a language-specific task adapter trained only on high-fertility language data (even with no direct supervision, via cross-lingual transfer) might outperform the shared adapter, meaning the standard practice of sharing doesn't just fail to help high-fertility languages but potentially leaves them worse off than a simpler alternative.

Token-count-equalized batching would indeed shift gradient dominance toward high-fertility languages — each high-fertility example contributes more tokens and therefore more gradient signal per example, so equalizing by tokens means seeing fewer high-fertility examples per batch, which reduces their raw update frequency but increases the semantic density per update, a trade-off that isn't obviously beneficial. The core problem is that token-level normalization conflates two different things: the number of decisions the model makes per example (proportional to tokens) and the amount of semantic content per example (roughly proportional to words or morphemes) — for a high-fertility language, token-equalizing batches means the model sees fewer complete sentences, potentially starving it of the discourse-level signal needed for tasks like NLI or reading comprehension where full-sentence context matters. Evidence from multilingual pretraining is instructive here: Conneau et al. (2020) with XLM-R used exponentially smoothed sampling (α=0.3) to upsample low-resource languages, which is example-level not token-level normalization, and found it improved low-resource performance but with diminishing returns — nobody has published a clean token-vs-example normalization ablation specifically for adapter training, which is a genuine gap. The relocation problem you identify is real and precise: token-equalizing batches would over-represent high-fertility language sentences in terms of gradient updates per semantic unit, because each token in a high-fertility language carries less meaning than each token in a low-fertility language, so you'd be amplifying noise rather than signal for those languages. What this suggests is that neither example-level nor token-level normalization is the right unit — the correct normalization target is probably morpheme or content-word equivalents, which requires either a separate morphological analyzer per language or a fertility-aware reweighting scheme that discounts tokens produced by over-segmentation, and building that requires solving a language-specific NLP problem before you can even begin adapter training.

Fertility asymmetry is genuinely symptomatic of a deeper mismatch: subword tokenization optimizes for compression efficiency on the training corpus, which means it implicitly encodes the resource distribution of that corpus into the model's atomic units — it's not a neutral preprocessing step but a architectural choice that bakes in who the model was built for. Character-level and byte-level models do sidestep fertility asymmetry in the specific sense that every language gets the same atomic unit size, but they trade it for a sequence length asymmetry that is arguably worse: ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022) processes raw UTF-8 bytes, which means a Chinese character that encodes a full morpheme costs 3 bytes while an ASCII character costs 1, and agglutinative languages with long words produce byte sequences 10-20x longer than their semantic content would suggest, pushing the effective context window problem from tokenization into raw sequence length. The evidence on whether byte-level models actually help low-resource languages is mixed: Xue et al. showed ByT5 outperforms mT5 on tasks requiring character-level sensitivity (spelling, morphology) and on some low-resource languages, but the gains are inconsistent and the model requires significantly more compute per example because attention complexity scales quadratically with sequence length — the languages that benefit most from byte-level processing are exactly the ones that produce the longest byte sequences and therefore cost the most to train on. CANINE (Clark et al., 2022) tried to address this with a strided local attention over characters followed by downsampling, achieving some compression before the deep transformer layers, but the downsampling itself reintroduces a granularity decision — you're choosing a pooling window that is again language-agnostic and therefore implicitly biased. The honest conclusion is that no current tokenization paradigm is neutral with respect to language resource distribution: subword models encode corpus skew into vocabulary, byte models encode it into compute requirements, and character models encode it into sequence structure — the asymmetry is conserved across representations, just displaced, because the underlying problem is that the languages differ fundamentally in their information-per-surface-unit density and no fixed atomic unit can equalize that without language-specific adaptation.
